_meta.source: The Muscle Ladder by Jeff Nippard
_meta.description: Deterministic rules library. Each rule has a trigger (condition), action (recommendation), and book_reference (chapter + short quote).

rules.name: Double progression
rules.rationale: Add reps within the target range first; when the top end is hit on all sets, add load and drop reps to the bottom.

book_reference.quote: Double progression — adding reps within a range before adding load — produces consistent progress without form breakdown.

rules.name: Beginner linear progression
rules.rationale: Beginners progress fastest with linear load increases each session until form fails.

book_reference.quote: Novices add weight nearly every session — they have not yet earned the right to need autoregulation.

rules.name: Stalled lifter — reps before load
rules.rationale: If load has stalled, accumulate reps before forcing more weight.

book_reference.quote: When the bar stops moving up, make it move more times before you try to move it up again.

rules.name: Stall + low RIR triggers deload
rules.rationale: Two weeks of stalled e1RM with RIR ≤ 1 indicates accumulated fatigue masking fitness gains. Deload one week.

book_reference.quote: When you stop progressing and feel beat up, you don't need more training — you need less.

rules.name: Adherence collapse triggers light week
rules.rationale: If life is overwhelming the plan, the plan must shrink — not the user's discipline.

book_reference.quote: Missed sessions are signal, not noise. The plan should bend before the lifter breaks.

rules.name: Programmed deload every 4-6 weeks
rules.rationale: Most intermediate lifters benefit from a planned deload every 4-6 weeks even without obvious stall.

book_reference.quote: A scheduled step back is cheaper than a forced one.

rules.name: Chest MEV/MAV/MRV
rules.rationale: Weekly hard sets per muscle: minimum effective ~8, maximum adaptive ~14, maximum recoverable ~22.

book_reference.quote: More sets work, until they don't. The MRV is the point where recovery breaks down.

rules.name: Back MEV/MAV/MRV
rules.rationale: Back tolerates and benefits from higher weekly volume than chest.

book_reference.quote: Back is famously volume-hungry — give it more sets than you give chest.

rules.name: Legs (quads) MEV/MAV/MRV
rules.rationale: Quads recover from less volume than back but more than smaller groups.

book_reference.quote: Heavy compound lower-body work generates outsized fatigue — count squat work cautiously.

rules.name: Biceps MEV/MAV/MRV
rules.rationale: Biceps already get indirect work from back movements — count those as 0.5 sets.

book_reference.quote: Indirect work counts. A row gives the biceps half a set whether you wanted it to or not.

rules.name: Triceps MEV/MAV/MRV
rules.rationale: Triceps also receive indirect work from all pressing movements.

book_reference.quote: If pressing volume is high, direct tricep work can stay low.

rules.name: Shoulders (side delts) MEV/MAV/MRV
rules.rationale: Side delts respond extremely well to high-frequency, high-volume work.

book_reference.quote: Side delts are nearly impossible to overtrain — train them frequently and with high reps.

rules.name: Junk volume warning
rules.rationale: Sets above MRV degrade recovery and add no hypertrophy.

book_reference.quote: Past MRV, every additional set is taxing recovery without adding stimulus.

rules.name: Below MEV halts growth
rules.rationale: If weekly volume is below MEV, the muscle stops growing.

book_reference.quote: The MEV is the floor — go below it and you maintain at best.

rules.name: Frequency: 2x per muscle minimum
rules.rationale: Each muscle group should be hit at least twice per week for optimal hypertrophy.

book_reference.quote: Hitting a muscle twice a week beats once-a-week-bro-splits for nearly all natural lifters.

rules.name: Compound first ordering
rules.rationale: Compound movements should appear early in the session when fatigue is lowest.

book_reference.quote: Big lifts go first. Fresh muscles move heavy weight; tired muscles waste it.

rules.name: Stretch-mediated hypertrophy
rules.rationale: Exercises that load the muscle in a stretched position (RDL, incline curl, deficit pushup) drive more hypertrophy per set.

book_reference.quote: Loading a muscle when it is lengthened is one of the most efficient hypertrophy levers we have.

rules.name: Shoulder impingement swap
rules.rationale: Landmine press has a more shoulder-friendly arc and reduces impingement risk.

book_reference.quote: If a movement hurts, find one that trains the same muscle without the hurt.

rules.name: Low-back swap for deadlift
rules.rationale: Trap bar deadlifts reduce lumbar shear stress while preserving most of the stimulus.

book_reference.quote: Trap bar deadlifts let you train heavy without forcing perfect spinal control under fatigue.

rules.name: Knee discomfort swap for squat
rules.rationale: Hack squats lock in a more knee-friendly torso angle and bar path.

book_reference.quote: Machine alternatives often produce the same growth with less joint cost.

rules.name: Antagonist balance
rules.rationale: Push and pull volume should be roughly balanced over the week to prevent posture issues and shoulder pain.

book_reference.quote: If you bench, you row. The body doesn't reward asymmetry.

rules.name: Hypertrophy rep range
rules.rationale: 6-15 reps to 0-2 RIR is the hypertrophy sweet spot for most exercises.

book_reference.quote: Effective reps live in the last few of any set near failure — most rep ranges work if you push them hard enough.

rules.name: Strength rep range
rules.rationale: 3-6 reps at moderate RIR builds maximal strength while preserving hypertrophy.

book_reference.quote: Lower reps build pure strength; higher reps build pure size; the middle does both.

rules.name: Compound RIR target
rules.rationale: Compounds carry more fatigue cost — leaving 1-2 reps in reserve preserves recovery.

book_reference.quote: On heavy compounds, the last rep is the most expensive — sometimes the smart move is to skip it.

rules.name: Isolation RIR target
rules.rationale: Isolations can be pushed closer to failure with minimal fatigue cost.

book_reference.quote: Curls and lateral raises taken to 0 RIR cost little and give a lot.

rules.name: BMR Mifflin-St Jeor (male)
rules.rationale: Most accurate BMR formula for general population per ISSN.

book_reference.quote: Mifflin-St Jeor is the consensus formula; old Harris-Benedict numbers run high.

rules.name: BMR Mifflin-St Jeor (female)
rules.rationale: Mifflin-St Jeor variant for biologically female individuals.

book_reference.quote: Use Mifflin for both sexes; the offset is the only difference.

rules.name: Cut deficit range
rules.rationale: 10-20% deficit preserves muscle while losing fat at a sustainable rate.

book_reference.quote: Bigger deficits don't lose more muscle — they just lose muscle faster.

rules.name: Lean bulk surplus
rules.rationale: Small surplus minimizes fat gain while supporting muscle synthesis.

book_reference.quote: You cannot build a kilogram of muscle from ten kilograms of food — anything above a modest surplus turns to fat.

rules.name: Recomp at maintenance
rules.rationale: Body recomposition works best at or near maintenance with high protein.

book_reference.quote: Recomp is real, but it is slow — most pronounced in new lifters or those returning from a layoff.

rules.name: Protein target
rules.rationale: 1.6-2.2 g/kg covers MPS needs for nearly all lifters; lean mass-based is more precise.

book_reference.quote: 1.6 g per kg is the floor for muscle building; above 2.2 yields diminishing returns.

rules.name: Fat target
rules.rationale: Fats below 0.6 g/kg risk hormonal disruption.

book_reference.quote: Cutting fats too low hurts testosterone and satiety; keep 0.8 g/kg as a floor.

rules.name: Cut: too-fast weight loss
rules.rationale: Losing >1% bodyweight per week increases muscle loss risk.

book_reference.quote: 0.5-1% of bodyweight per week is the sweet spot — faster than that and you bleed muscle.

rules.name: Cut: stalled weight loss
rules.rationale: Two flat weeks indicates the deficit has shrunk via TDEE adaptation.

book_reference.quote: TDEE drifts down as you lose weight — you must drift calories down with it.

rules.name: Diet break protocol
rules.rationale: Strategic diet breaks at maintenance restore hormones and adherence.

book_reference.quote: A week at maintenance every 8-12 weeks gives your body — and your willpower — a chance to reset.

rules.name: Lean bulk: too-fast weight gain
rules.rationale: Gaining >0.5% bodyweight/week is overwhelmingly fat.

book_reference.quote: Beyond about 0.25-0.5% per week, you're not building muscle faster — just gaining fat faster.

rules.name: Adherence collapse — simplify
rules.rationale: Low adherence indicates the plan is too complex or restrictive.

book_reference.quote: The best diet is the one you actually follow — complexity is the enemy of consistency.

rules.name: Sleep target
rules.rationale: Sleep below 7 hours suppresses MPS and increases cortisol.

book_reference.quote: Sleep is the most underrated anabolic in the toolkit; nothing replaces it.

rules.name: Soreness interpretation
rules.rationale: Soreness lasting >3 days indicates excessive volume or eccentric overload.

book_reference.quote: Soreness is a poor measure of growth — but persistent soreness is a clear measure of overreach.

rules.name: 48-hour same-muscle rule
rules.rationale: Hitting the same muscle on consecutive days compromises recovery for both sessions.

book_reference.quote: 48 hours between same-muscle sessions is the minimum for meaningful recovery.

rules.name: Ego lifting warning

action.message: Form likely breaking down — drop 10% load.

rules.rationale: Consistently failing reps with bad form indicates ego lifting.

book_reference.quote: If you have to cheat the weight up, the weight isn't yours yet.

rules.name: Program hopping

action.message: Stick with the plan for 6+ weeks before judging it.

rules.rationale: Programs need 6-8 weeks to express their results.

book_reference.quote: Stop switching programs every two weeks — no plan can prove itself in fourteen days.

rules.name: Excessive cardio in a bulk

action.message: High cardio volume conflicts with hypertrophy — cap at 2-3 short sessions.

rules.rationale: Excessive cardio interferes with muscle protein synthesis recovery.

book_reference.quote: Cardio doesn't kill gains; too much cardio kills gains.

rules.name: Skipping legs

action.message: Lower body undertrained — add at least one leg session.

rules.rationale: Leg training drives systemic hormonal response and total muscle balance.

book_reference.quote: Skipping legs isn't a meme — it's a measurable loss in your total muscle mass potential.

rules.name: Session length cap
rules.rationale: Sessions over 90 minutes show diminishing returns and elevated cortisol.

book_reference.quote: Past 75-90 minutes, you're paying recovery debt for marginal new stimulus.

rules.name: Rest interval — compounds
rules.rationale: Compounds need 2-3 minutes rest for full ATP recovery.

book_reference.quote: Short rests on big lifts cost you reps — and reps are the currency of growth.

rules.name: Rest interval — isolations
rules.rationale: Isolations recover faster — 60-90s rest preserves intensity without inflating session length.

book_reference.quote: Curls don't need three-minute rests; that time is better spent on the next set.

rules.name: RIR drift — increase load
rules.rationale: RIR consistently ≥ 3 indicates the weight is too light.

book_reference.quote: If you finish every set with three reps in the tank, you're warming up, not training.

rules.name: Negative RIR pattern — reduce load
rules.rationale: Consistent 0 RIR with form breakdown signals overreach on the working weight.

book_reference.quote: Three sessions in a row at failure usually means the weight, not the lifter, is the problem.

rules.name: Activity factor — sedentary
rules.rationale: Sedentary lifestyle plus training: 1.4× BMR.

book_reference.quote: Sedentary doesn't mean lazy — it means non-training movement is minimal.

rules.name: Activity factor — light
rules.rationale: Light daily activity plus training: 1.55× BMR.

book_reference.quote: A daily walk and gym training puts most people here.

rules.name: Activity factor — moderate
rules.rationale: Moderate daily activity: 1.65× BMR.

book_reference.quote: Moderate means consistently active outside the gym — most service workers fit here.

rules.name: Activity factor — active
rules.rationale: Very active daily life plus training: 1.75× BMR.

book_reference.quote: Physical jobs and daily cardio land you in the active band.

rules.name: Refeed day
rules.rationale: Strategic carb refeed restores leptin and training performance.

book_reference.quote: A one-day carb refeed every couple of weeks helps adherence more than physiology, but both matter.

rules.name: ROM — full range preferred
rules.rationale: Full range of motion produces more hypertrophy than partials in nearly every comparison.

book_reference.quote: Train the muscle through every degree it owns — not just the comfortable ones.

rules.name: Free weight vs machine
rules.rationale: Machines reduce stability cost, letting beginners learn movement patterns safely.

book_reference.quote: Machines aren't training wheels — they're tools that let you focus on the muscle, not the balance.
